page.title: tinyactors: like SQLite, but for actors
page.description: tinyactors runs millions of statecharts inside your program, in Node.js, Python, a browser or C: composable state machines that describe a reactive system formally.

hero.headline: Like SQLite, but for actors
hero.lede: tinyactors runs millions of statecharts inside your program, in Node.js, Python, a browser or C. A statechart is a composable state machine that describes a reactive system formally and is easy to verify.

section.heading: Write each actor's behavior as one chart
section.p: Each statechart runs as an actor: it keeps its own data and handles one event at a time.
An Erlang or Akka actor runs any code you give it. A tinyactors actor runs a chart, with every state and transition written down.

section.heading: Hand a chart to a coding agent
section.p: Statecharts date from 1987, but writing every state down by hand was more work than most teams would take on.
A coding agent does that work for you. In return it gets an actor's whole behavior in one file instead of a call graph.
The chart sends an event for every effect, and your code performs it. A simulated clock runs its timeouts, so the agent tests each change in milliseconds.

section.heading: Run millions of actors in your process

claim.p: tinyactors is a library on your own event loop, so your actors deploy with your program.

claim.statement: One chart runs in JavaScript, Python and C
claim.p: Each language's package wraps one C core, and that core passes all 191 automatic tests of the W3C's SCXML suite.
claim.source: One test suite for every package

claim.statement: Small enough for every part of a system
claim.p: An actor takes about 530 bytes in Node.js, and one saved to a database while idle keeps about 120.

section.heading: Kill your unit tests
section.p: A unit test checks one run you wrote down. A property is a rule, like "never charge a card more than three times", checked on runs a program generates.

section.heading: Build a team chat
section.p: A chat's hard part is its state: who is in which room, and who is online as people come and go.
In the tutorial's five steps, each part of that state lives in an actor:

item.text: Joins and posts arrive at the same time, and the member list must stay right. Each room is an actor that keeps its members and handles one join or post at a time, in the order they arrive.
A user who goes quiet must turn away, though no event says so. Each user's chart is offline, active or away, and a timer turns an active user away after 300 seconds without activity.
Most users sit idle, but their state must survive until they return. A user at rest is saved to a store and woken by its next event, so a thousand users run with fifty in memory.
Running actors move to their chart's next version and keep the state they reached.
A process holding two million actors copies into a 165 MB snapshot that another process restores.
Each step an actor takes becomes a span in your OpenTelemetry collector.
